{{ProbabilityTopics}}

In [[probability]] and [[statistics]], a '''factorial moment measure''' is a [[mathematical]] quantity, [[Function (mathematics)|function]] or, more precisely, [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]]  that is defined in relation to [[mathematical objects]] known as [[point process]]es, which are types of [[stochastic processes]] often used as [[mathematical model]]s of physical phenomena representable as [[random]]ly positioned [[Point (geometry)|points]] in [[time]], [[space]] or both. Moment measures generalize the idea of [[factorial moment]]s, which are useful for studying [[non-negative]] [[integer]]-valued [[random variables]].<ref name="daleyPPI2003">D. J. Daley and D. Vere-Jones. ''An introduction to the theory of point processes. Vol. I''. Probability and its Applications (New York). Springer, New York, second edition, 2003.

</ref>

The first factorial moment measure of a point process coincides with its [[Moment measure#First moment measure|first moment measure]] or ''intensity measure'',<ref name="BB1"/> which gives the [[Expected value|expected]]  or [[average]] number of points of the point process located in some region of space. In general, if the number of points in some region is considered as a random variable, then the moment factorial measure of this region is the factorial moment of this random variable.<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic">D. Stoyan, W. S. Kendall, J. Mecke, and L. Ruschendorf. ''Stochastic geometry and its applications'', volume 2. Wiley Chichester, 1995.</ref>  Factorial moment measures completely characterize a wide class of point processes, which means they can be used to uniquely identify a point process.

If a factorial moment measure is [[absolutely continuous]], then with respect to the [[Lebesgue measure]] it is said to have a ''density'' (which is a generalized form of a [[derivative]]), and this density is known by a number of names such as '''factorial moment density''' and '''product density''',  as well as ''coincidence density'',<ref name="daleyPPI2003"/> ''joint intensity''<ref name="hough2006determinantal">{{cite journal
| last1=Hough | first1=J. Ben
| last2=Krishnapur | first2=Manjunath
| last3=Peres | first3=Yuval | author-link3=Yuval Peres
| last4=Virág | first4=Bálint | author-link4=Bálint Virág
| title=Determinantal processes and independence
| journal=Probability Surveys
| date=2006
| volume=3
| pages=206–229
| doi=10.1214/154957806000000078
| arxiv=math/0503110
| s2cid=9604112}}</ref>
,  ''correlation function'' or ''multivariate frequency spectrum''<ref name="handa2009two">K. Handa. The two-parameter {Poisson-Dirichlet} point process. ''Bernoulli'', 15(4):1082–1116, 2009.

</ref> The first and second factorial moment densities of a point process are used in the definition of the ''pair correlation function'', which gives a way to statistically quantify the strength of interaction or [[correlation]] between points of a point process.<ref name="baddeley2007spatial">A. Baddeley, I. B{\'a}r{\'a}ny, and R. Schneider. Spatial point processes and their applications. ''Stochastic Geometry: Lectures given at the CIME Summer School held in Martina Franca, Italy, September 13–18, 2004'', pages 1–75, 2007.

</ref>

Factorial moment measures serve as useful tools in the study of point processes<ref name="daleyPPI2003"/><ref name="baddeley2007spatial"/><ref name="daleyPPII2008">D. J. Daley and D. Vere-Jones. ''An introduction to the theory of point processes. Vol. {II''}. Probability and its Applications (New York). Springer, New York, second edition, 2008</ref> as well as the related fields of [[stochastic geometry]]<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/> and [[spatial statistics]],<ref name="baddeley2007spatial"/><ref name="moller2003statistical">{{Cite book | last1 = Møller | first1 = Jesper | last2 = Waagepetersen | first2 = Rasmus Plenge | doi = 10.1201/9780203496930 | title = Statistical Inference and Simulation for Spatial Point Processes | series = C&H/CRC Monographs on Statistics & Applied Probability | volume = 100 | year = 2003 | isbn = 978-1-58488-265-7 }}</ref> which are applied in various [[scientific]] and [[engineering]] disciplines such as [[biology]], [[geology]], [[physics]], and [[telecommunications]].<ref name="daleyPPI2003"/><ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/><ref name="BB2"/>

==Point process notation==
{{Main|Point process notation}}

Point processes are mathematical objects that are defined on some underlying [[mathematical space]]. Since these processes are often used to represent collections of points randomly scattered in space, time or both, the underlying space is usually ''d''-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] denoted here by '''R'''<sup>d</sup>, but they can be defined on more [[Abstraction (mathematics)|abstract]] mathematical spaces.<ref name="daleyPPII2008"/>

Point processes have a number of interpretations, which is reflected by the various types of [[point process notation]].<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/><ref name="BB2">F. Baccelli and B. Błaszczyszyn. ''Stochastic Geometry and Wireless Networks, Volume II – Applications'', volume 4, No 1–2 of ''Foundations and Trends in Networking''. NoW Publishers, 2009.

</ref>  For example, if a point <math>\textstyle x</math> belongs to or is a member of a point process, denoted by ''N'', then this can be written as:<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/>

: <math>\textstyle x\in {N},</math>

and represents the point process being interpreted as a random [[Set (mathematics)|set]]. Alternatively, the number of points of ''N'' located in some [[Borel set]] ''B'' is often written as:<ref name="BB1"/><ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/><ref name="moller2003statistical"/>

: <math>\textstyle {N}(B), </math>

which reflects a [[random measure]] interpretation for point processes. These two notations are often used in parallel or interchangeably.<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/><ref name="moller2003statistical"/><ref name="BB1">{{cite journal|last1=Baccelli|first1=François|title=Stochastic Geometry and Wireless Networks: Volume I Theory|journal=Foundations and Trends in Networking|volume=3|issue=3–4|year=2009|pages=249–449|issn=1554-057X|doi=10.1561/1300000006|url=https://hal.inria.fr/inria-00403039/file/FnT1.pdf}}</ref>

==Definitions==

===''n''-th factorial power of a point process===

For some positive [[integer]] <math>\textstyle n=1,2,\ldots</math>, the <math>\textstyle n</math>-th factorial power of a point process <math>\textstyle {N}</math> on <math>\textstyle \textbf{R}^d</math> is defined as:<ref name="BB1"/>

:<math> {N}^{(n)}(B_1\times\cdots\times B_n)= \sum_{(x_1\neq\dots\neq x_n)\in {N} } \prod_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}_{B_i}(x_i) </math>

where <math>\textstyle B_1,...,B_n</math> is a collection of not necessarily [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] Borel sets in <math>\textstyle \textbf{R}^d</math>, which form an <math>\textstyle n</math>-fold [[Cartesian product]] of sets denoted by:

:<math> B_1\times\cdots\times B_n.</math>

The symbol <math>\textstyle \mathbf{1}</math> denotes an [[indicator function]] such that <math>\textstyle \mathbf{1}_{B_1} </math> is a [[Dirac measure]] for the set <math>\textstyle B_n</math>. The [[summation]] in the above expression is performed over all <math>\textstyle n</math>-[[tuples]] of distinct points, including [[permutations]], which can be contrasted with the definition of the [[Moment measure#n-th power of a point process|''n''-th power of a point process]]. The symbol  <math>\textstyle \Pi</math> denotes  [[multiplication#Capital Pi notation|multiplication]] while the existence of various [[point process notation]] means that the ''n''-th factorial power of a point process is sometimes defined using other notation.<ref name="BB1"/>

===''n''-th factorial moment measure===

The ''n''-th factorial moment measure or ''n''-th order factorial moment measure is defined as:

:<math> M^{(n)}(B_1\times\cdots\times B_n)=E [{N}^{(n)}(B_1\times\cdots\times B_n)], </math>

where the ''E'' denotes the [[Expected value|expectation]] ([[Operator (mathematics)#Probability theory|operator]]) of the point process ''N''. In other words, the ''n''-th factorial moment measure is the expectation of the ''n''-th factorial power of some point process.

The ''n''-th factorial moment measure of a point process ''N'' is equivalently defined<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/> by:

:<math> \int_{\textbf{R}^{n d}}f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)  M^{(n)}(dx_1,\ldots,dx_n)=E \left[ \sum_{(x_1\neq\cdots\neq x_n)\in {N} } f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)   \right], </math>

where <math> f</math> is any non-negative [[measurable function]] on <math> \textbf{R}^{n d}</math>, and the above summation is performed over all <math>n</math> tuples of distinct points, including permutations. Consequently, the factorial moment measure is defined such that there are no points repeating in the product set,  as opposed to the moment measure.<ref name="daleyPPII2008"/>

===First factorial moment measure===

The first factorial moment measure <math>\textstyle M^1</math> coincides with the [[Moment measure#First moment measure|first moment measure]]:<ref name="BB1"/>

:<math> M^{(1)}(B)=M^1(B)=E [{N}(B)], </math>

where <math>\textstyle M^1</math> is known, among other terms, as the ''intensity measure''<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/> or ''mean measure'',<ref name="kingman1992poisson">J. F. C. Kingman. ''Poisson processes'', volume 3. Oxford university press, 1992.

</ref> and is interpreted as the expected number of points of <math>\textstyle {N}</math> found or located in the set <math>\textstyle B</math>

===Second factorial moment measure===

The second factorial moment measure for two Borel sets <math>\textstyle A</math> and <math>\textstyle B</math> is:

:<math> M^{(2)}(A\times B)=M^2(A\times B)-M^1(A\cap B). </math>

==Name explanation==

For some Borel set <math>\textstyle B</math>, the namesake of this measure is revealed when the <math>\textstyle n\,</math>th factorial moment measure reduces to:

:<math> M^{(n)}(B\times\cdots\times B)=E [{N}(B)({N}(B)-1)\cdots ({N}(B)-n+1)], </math>

which is the <math>\textstyle n\,</math>-th [[factorial moment]] of the random variable <math>\textstyle {N}(B)</math>.<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/>

==Factorial moment density==

If a factorial moment measure is [[absolutely continuous]], then it has a density (or more precisely, a [[Radon–Nikodym derivative]] or density) with respect to the [[Lebesgue measure]] and this density is known as the ''factorial moment density'' or ''product density'', ''joint intensity'', ''correlation function'', or ''multivariate frequency spectrum''. Denoting the <math>\textstyle n</math>-th factorial moment density by <math>\textstyle \mu^{(n)}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math>,  it is defined in respect to the equation:<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/>

:<math> M^{(n)}(B_1\times\ldots\times B_n)=\int_{B_1}\cdots\int_{B_n}\mu^{(n)}(x_1,\ldots,x_n) dx_1\cdots dx_n. </math>

Furthermore, this means the following expression

:<math> E \left[ \sum_{(x_1\neq\cdots\neq x_n)\in {N} } f(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \right]= \int_{\textbf{R}^{n d}} f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)  \mu^{(n)}(x_1,\ldots,x_n) dx_1\cdots dx_n, </math>

where <math>\textstyle f</math> is any non-negative [[Bounded function|bounded]] measurable function defined on <math>\textstyle \textbf{R}^{ n}</math>.

==Pair correlation function==
In spatial statistics and stochastic geometry, to measure the statistical [[Correlation and dependence|correlation]] relationship between points of a point process, the ''pair correlation function'' of a point process <math>{N}</math> is defined as:<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/><ref name="baddeley2007spatial"/>

:<math> \rho(x_1,x_2)=\frac{\mu^{(2)}(x_1,x_2)}{\mu^{(1)}(x_1) \mu^{(1)}(x_2) }, </math>

where the points <math>x_1,x_2\in R^d </math>. In general, <math>\rho(x_1,x_2)\geq 0</math> whereas  <math>\rho(x_1,x_2)=1</math> corresponds to no correlation (between points) in the typical statistical sense.<ref name="baddeley2007spatial"/>

==Examples==

===Poisson point process===

For a [[Poisson point process#General Poisson point process|general Poisson point process]] with intensity measure <math>\textstyle \Lambda</math> the <math>\textstyle n</math>-th factorial moment measure is given by the expression:<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/>

:<math> M^{(n)}(B_1\times\cdots\times B_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n[\Lambda(B_i)], </math>

where <math>\textstyle \Lambda</math> is the intensity measure or first moment measure of <math>\textstyle {N}</math>, which for some Borel set <math>\textstyle B</math> is given by:

:<math> \Lambda(B)=M^1(B)=E[{N}(B)]. </math>

For a [[Poisson point process#Homogeneous Poisson point process|homogeneous Poisson point process]]  the <math>\textstyle n</math>-th factorial moment measure is simply:<ref name="BB1"/>

:<math> M^{(n)}(B_1\times\cdots\times B_n)=\lambda^n \prod_{i=1}^n |B_i|, </math>

where <math>\textstyle |B_i|</math> is the length, area, or volume (or more generally, the [[Lebesgue measure]]) of <math>\textstyle B_i</math>.  Furthermore, the <math>\textstyle n</math>-th factorial moment density is:<ref name="stoyan1995stochastic"/>

:<math> \mu^{(n)}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\lambda^n. </math>

The pair-correlation function of the homogeneous Poisson point process is simply

:<math> \rho(x_1,x_2)=1, </math>

which reflects the lack of interaction between points of this point process.

==Factorial moment expansion==

The expectations of general [[Functional (mathematics)|functional]]s of simple point processes, provided some certain mathematical conditions, have (possibly infinite) expansions or [[Series (mathematics)|series]] consisting of the corresponding factorial moment measures.<ref name="fme">B. Blaszczyszyn. Factorial-moment expansion for stochastic systems. ''Stoch. Proc. Appl.'', 56:321–335, 1995.

</ref><ref name="fme_marked">{{cite journal
| last1=Kroese | first1=Dirk P.
| last2=Schmidt | first2=Volker
| title=Light-traffic analysis for queues with spatially distributed arrivals
| journal=[[Mathematics of Operations Research]]
| volume=21
| issue=1
| pages=135–157
| date=1996
| doi=10.1287/moor.21.1.135| url=https://research.utwente.nl/en/publications/fa8c87ca-53a1-4369-a765-9f7d39a19654
}}

</ref> In comparison to the [[Taylor series]], which consists of a series of [[derivative]]s of some function, the ''n''th factorial moment measure plays the roll as that of the ''n'' th derivative the Taylor series.  In other words, given a general functional ''f'' of some simple point process, then this [[Taylor's theorem|Taylor-like theorem]] for non-Poisson point processes means an expansion exists for the expectation of the function ''E'', provided some mathematical condition is satisfied, which ensures convergence of the expansion.
